parts.title: Where do RXFP3 cells in different parts of the lateral hypothalamus and zona incerta send their nerve fibres?
parts.abstract:
RXFP3 is a receptor, a protein on the surface of nerve cells that catches a chemical signal. It belongs to a family called the relaxin family peptide receptors. It is switched on by a small signalling molecule called relaxin-3, which has stayed much the same over the course of evolution. RXFP3 is a type of receptor known as a G-protein coupled receptor.

We recently showed that we could switch on a group of RXFP3-carrying cells in two brain regions, the lateral hypothalamus and the zona incerta, using a drug that acts on a genetically engineered receptor. We call these cells LH/ZIRXFP3. After the mice had learned to fear a particular place, switching on these cells made some of them jump as if trying to escape. This happened in only some of the mice.

The lateral hypothalamus and the zona incerta are made up of many different kinds of nerve cells, and their nerve fibres reach many different places. So we thought that the LH/ZIRXFP3 cells might be split into separate groups, each with its own pattern of connections, and that each group might control a different part of how an animal defends itself.

To test this idea, we used a special virus that carries a glowing tracer. The tracer only switches on in cells that carry a gene called Cre, and it travels forward along the nerve fibres to show where they go. We injected small amounts of this tracer into one of four different spots in the lateral hypothalamus and zona incerta of mice that carry the Cre gene. We then mapped where the fibres went across the whole brain.

Each injection spot produced its own pattern of connections, especially to brain regions known to be involved in threats and defence. Two patterns stood out. Fibres from the front part of the zona incerta and the front part of the lateral hypothalamus went strongly to the lateral habenula, a small brain region that helps process negative feelings. Fibres from the middle and back parts of the zona incerta went to the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray, a region in the brainstem that helps control escape and defensive reactions.

We also used a second tracer that travels backward along nerve fibres, together with a method called RNAscope that makes the genetic messages of particular genes glow. This showed that most of the LH/ZIRXFP3 fibres going to the lateral habenula came from a subset of lateral hypothalamus cells that make the chemical messenger glutamate (vGlut2). Most of the fibres going to the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray came from a subset of zona incerta cells that make the enzyme GAD1, which is used to make the calming chemical messenger GABA.

Taken together, our results strongly suggest that LH/ZIRXFP3 cells send their nerve fibres to different places across the brain depending on where they sit within these brain regions. This likely reflects the many different jobs these nerve cells do.

Supplementary Information

Extra material for this paper is available online at https://doi.org/10.1007/s00429-026-03146-0.
parts.introduction_first:
The zona incerta is a small brain region that sits just below the thalamus, a large relay station in the middle of the brain. Most of its nerve cells use GABA, a chemical messenger that calms other cells down. The region is made up of several groups of cells that differ in their chemistry, and these groups are mixed together in no simple order. Their nerve fibres also reach many different places, both sending signals out and receiving signals in (Arena et al. 2024; Mitrofanis 2005).

Because of this, it is not surprising that scientists have never agreed on what the zona incerta does. The region was named the 'zone of uncertainty' by Forel in 1877, and that name has stuck. Studies have linked it to many kinds of behaviour. These include sleep (Blanco-Centurion et al. 2023; Vidal-Ortiz et al. 2024; Zhu et al. 2025), movement (Richards et al. 2025; Sharma et al. 2024), pain (Li et al. 2023; Singh et al. 2022; Wang et al. 2020a), social behaviour (Li et al. 2024), searching for food (Ye et al. 2023), and several parts of fear and defence (Li et al. 2021; Lin et al. 2023; Richards et al. 2025; Venkataraman et al. 2019, 2021). With so many roles and such a varied make-up, the zona incerta may work as a centre that gathers information from the senses and turns it into the right behaviour (Wang et al. 2019).
parts.introduction_rest:
Many studies have started to work out what the different groups of nerve cells in the zona incerta do, based on the chemical messengers they use. However, these studies usually treat the whole region as one group. They do not ask whether different parts of the region might have their own separate jobs.

Each part of the zona incerta has its own pattern of nerve fibres, with its own connections to other brain regions (Arena et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2022). So if we study all the cells of one chemical type together, without paying attention to where they sit, we are likely to miss some of the finer details of what the region does. For example, a recent study looked at two subsets of GABA-using nerve cells in the zona incerta, each found in a different part of the region. These two subsets sent their nerve fibres to different places. They also played different parts in feeding and in switching between sleep and waking (Zhu et al. 2025).

Sorting the cells of a given chemical type by where they sit within the region may tell us more about what the zona incerta does. It may also help explain why scientists have given this region so many roles that seem to clash with one another.

In mice, a group of nerve cells that carry the RXFP3 receptor is spread across several parts of the zona incerta and into the neighbouring lateral hypothalamus (Ma et al. 2007; Richards et al. 2025; Smith et al. 2010). RXFP3 is a G-protein coupled receptor of a type called Gi/o. It is the receptor that relaxin-3 attaches to (Bathgate et al. 2006). Relaxin-3 is a small signalling molecule that has stayed much the same over the course of evolution. Most of it is made by nerve cells in a brainstem region called the pontine nucleus incertus (Burazin et al. 2002; Ma et al. 2007). These cells have also been shown to send nerve fibres to the lateral hypothalamus and zona incerta (Nasirova et al. 2020).

We recently showed that the LH/ZIRXFP3 cells send their nerve fibres to several brain regions that are thought to be involved in learning fear and in defensive behaviour. The most important of these are the lateral habenula, the periaqueductal gray and the nucleus reuniens, a small region in the middle of the thalamus (Richards et al. 2025). However, when we switched on these cells while the mice were remembering a fear they had learned, the mice froze less. In some of the mice, though, the cells made them jump as if trying to escape.

This led us to suggest that the LH/ZIRXFP3 cells might be split into separate groups, each controlling a different kind of response to a threat. In this study, we show that groups of LH/ZIRXFP3 cells sitting in different parts of the region send their nerve fibres to different places across the brain. This is especially true for key regions involved in fear and defensive behaviour. These findings give the first full map of where the RXFP3-carrying cells in the lateral hypothalamus and zona incerta send their fibres. They give future studies a solid starting point for working out what each group does.

## Materials and methods

### The mice we used

We carried out all our experiments under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act (2004). We followed the National Health and Medical Research Council Code of Practice for the Care and Use of Animals for Experimental Purposes in Australia (8th Edition, 2013). The Macquarie University Animal Ethics Committee approved the work (Animal Research Authority number: 2021/021).

We used adult mice aged 8–13 weeks that carry the Cre gene (RXFP3-Cre mice; Ch’ng et al. 2019; Richards et al. 2025). These mice are inbred, which means they come from a family line bred for many generations so that they are all genetically very similar. In total we used 21 female and 13 male mice.

The mice lived in groups of 2–4 in cages, each with its own ventilation system. They had 12 hours of light and 12 hours of darkness each day, with the lights coming on at 6 am. The room was kept at 21 °C, give or take 1 °C, and the mice had nesting material and could eat standard food and drink water whenever they wanted. We left seven mice (6 female, 3 male) out of the final analyses because the virus had been injected in the wrong place.

### Surgery to place the tracers

We put the mice to sleep with the anaesthetic gas isoflurane (5% by volume in oxygen, kept at 0.5%–2%). We then placed each mouse in a stereotaxic frame (David Kopf Instruments, CA, USA). This is a device that holds the head still and lets us measure exactly where to put a needle. Before surgery, each mouse received a painkiller called carprofen (5 mg per kg of body weight, injected under the skin; Rimadyl, Zoetis Australia). It is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, the same family as ibuprofen.

To follow fibres forward, we injected the tracer into one side of the brain only. We used 25 nL of virus, injected at 1 nL per second. A nanolitre (nL) is a billionth of a litre, so this is a very tiny amount. The virus was AAV-DJ-hSyn-FLEX-mGFP-synaptophysin-mRuby, diluted 1:10 in salt water (saline) to 3 × 10^13 GC/mL. It came from Professor Andrew Allen at The University of Melbourne (Beier et al. 2015). GC stands for genome copies, a measure of how much virus is in a liquid.

We injected at one of four spots in the lateral hypothalamus and zona incerta. Each spot is described by three positions measured from a standard starting point in the brain. A/P is the position from front to back, M/L is the position from side to side, and D/V is the position from top to bottom. The front part of the lateral hypothalamus (ALH) was at A/P −1.00 mm, M/L 1.25 mm, D/V −5.05 mm. The front part of the zona incerta (ZIR) was at A/P −0.95 mm, M/L 0.75 mm, D/V −4.55 mm. The middle part of the zona incerta (ZII) was at A/P −1.60 mm, M/L 1.00 mm, D/V −4.50 mm. The back part of the zona incerta (ZIC) was at A/P −2.25 mm, M/L 1.70 mm, D/V −4.15 mm.

To follow fibres backward, we again injected one side of the brain only. This time we used 40 nL of a second virus, injected at 1 nL per second. The virus was pENN.AAV.hSyn.HI.eGFP-Cre.WPRE-SV40 (2.1 × 10^13 GC/mL; Addgene, 105540-AAVrg). We placed it in one of two brainstem regions. The first was the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray, at a 20° angle to the side, A/P −4.30 mm, M/L 0.35 mm, D/V −2.85 mm. The second was the lateral habenula, also at a 20° angle to the side, A/P −1.80 mm, M/L 0.45 mm, D/V −2.80 mm.

During surgery, we dripped lidocaine, a local anaesthetic, onto the spot being operated on. After the virus had been injected, we left the fine glass tube (the micropipette) in place for 10 minutes. We then raised it by 0.1 mm and left it for another minute before taking it out. We gave the injections with a Nanoject III Auto-Nanoliter Injector (3-000-207; Drummond Scientific Company, PA, USA).

### Preparing the brains and slicing them

We waited two weeks after the injections so that the virus had time to get into the cells. Then we put all the mice to sleep with sodium pentobarbitone (80 mg per kg, injected into the belly; Virbac, Australia).

For the experiments that followed fibres forward, we first flushed the blood out of the brain. We did this by pumping fluid through the heart, a method called transcardial perfusion. We used heparinised saline, which is salt water with a substance added to stop clotting, at 7 ml per minute for 2 minutes. We then pumped 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in 0.1 M phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for 5 minutes. PFA is a chemical that preserves tissue, and PBS is a gentle salt solution.

We removed the brains and kept them in 4% PFA in 0.1 M PBS for 1 hour. Next we washed them in 0.1 M PBS for 1 hour. Then we placed them overnight in 30% sucrose (sugar) in 0.1 M PBS, which protects the brain from freezing damage. We froze the brains quickly over dry ice and cut them into thin slices, 40 µm thick, on a Leica CM1950 Cryostat (Leica Biosystems, Germany). A micrometre (µm) is a thousandth of a millimetre. We cut the slices front to back, which is called coronally. We kept every fourth slice in sodium azide (0.1% in 0.1 M PBS) at 4 °C.

For the experiments that followed fibres backward, we gave the mice a second dose of sodium pentobarbitone (100 mg per kg, injected into the belly; Virbac, Australia) to end their lives humanely. We then removed the brains and froze them fresh over dry ice. We cut them coronally into slices 8 µm thick on the same Leica CM1950 Cryostat. We placed the slices on Superfrost™ Plus slides (Epredia, NH, USA) and stored them at −80 °C until we needed them for RNAscope and for antibody staining.

### Antibody staining (immunohistochemistry)

For the experiments that followed fibres forward, we stained every fourth slice across the whole brain with glowing antibodies. Antibodies are proteins that stick to one particular target. We used them to make the tracer’s own glow stand out more strongly. The tracer’s own glow comes from two parts. One is mGFP, a green glowing protein. The other is mRuby, a red glowing protein. We followed the methods described before (Walker et al. 2017), with the right changes to the antibodies (Table 1).

### RNAscope combined with antibody staining

For the experiments that followed fibres backward, we combined RNAscope with antibody staining. This let us find exactly where the LH/ZIRXFP3 cells that send fibres to the lateral habenula and the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray come from. It also showed what kind of chemical messengers they use.

We took the slides out of the −80 °C freezer. We fixed the slices in 4% PFA in PBS for 15 minutes at room temperature, then washed them twice in 0.1 M PBS (1 minute each, at room temperature). After drying, we drew a water-repelling barrier around each slice. This stops the liquid from running between neighbouring slices. We then treated the slices with a protease (Protease Plus), an enzyme that loosens the tissue, for 10 minutes in a damp place at 40 °C. After that we washed them twice with distilled water (dH2O).

We used the RNAscope® Multiplex Fluorescent V2 Assay (ACDBio, USA). This method labels the genetic messages (mRNA) of chosen genes with glowing probes. We ran two versions. Run 1 labelled the messages for Rxfp3 and Slc17a6. Run 2 labelled the messages for Rxfp3 and Gad1. Rxfp3 is the gene that makes the RXFP3 receptor. Slc17a6 is a gene that cells use to make glutamate, and Gad1 is the gene for the enzyme that makes GABA. We kept all later steps in a damp place at 40 °C.

We rinsed the slices twice with wash buffer (0.1 × saline sodium citrate, 0.03% sodium dodecyl sulfate in dH2O). Then we added the probes and left them for 90 minutes. The probes were for Rxfp3 (Mm-Rxfp3-C2, #439381-C2; both runs), Slc17a6 (Mm-Slc17a6, #319171; run 1) and Gad1 (Mm-Gad1-C3, #400951-C3; run 2). On some slices we also added two control probes. One was a mouse-specific positive control probe (RNAscope® 3-plex Positive Control Probe-Mm, #320881). The other was a universal negative control probe (RNAscope® 3-plex Negative Control Probe, #320871).

Next we added three amplifying steps, called Amp1 (30 minutes), Amp2 (30 minutes) and Amp3 (15 minutes), to make the target probes stronger. We rinsed the slices in wash buffer after each Amp step (2 × 2 minutes).

To make the Slc17a6 probe glow, we then added HRP C1 (15 minutes), Opal 690 (Akoya Biosciences, #FP1497001KT; 1:2000) and an HRP blocker (15 minutes). HRP is an enzyme that the probe uses to build up a coloured product. Opal 690 is a dye that glows when it is lit. To make the Rxfp3 probe glow, we then added HRP C2 (15 minutes), Opal 570 (Akoya Biosciences, #FP1488022KT; 1:1000) and an HRP blocker.

Run 2 worked the other way round. We first added HRP C2, Opal 570 (1:1000) and an HRP blocker to make the Rxfp3 signal. Then we added HRP C3, Opal 690 (1:2000) and an HRP blocker to make the Gad1 signal.

For both runs, we then added the chicken anti-GFP polyclonal primary antibody (1:150; Abcam, ab113; RRID:AB_297905) for 90 minutes at room temperature. We washed the slices twice in 0.1 M PBS (2 × 2 minutes, at room temperature). Then we added the AF-488-conjugated anti-chicken IgG raised in donkey secondary antibody (1:75; Jackson ImmunoResearch; 703–545-155, RRID:AB_2340375). This made the eGFP tag on the backward-tracing virus glow.

We washed the slices twice in 0.1 M PBS (2 × 2 minutes, at room temperature). Then we sealed them under a thin glass cover with Fluoroshield™ with DAPI mounting medium (Sigma-Aldrich, MI, USA). DAPI is a dye that makes the cell nuclei glow blue. We left the slides to dry overnight in the dark and stored them at 4 °C until we took pictures. Unless we say otherwise, all RNAscope® chemicals came from Advanced Cell Diagnostics, USA.

### Taking pictures with the microscope

For the experiments that followed fibres forward, we first took overview pictures of the slices. We used an Olympus SLIDEVIEW™ VS200 Slide Scanner (Olympus/Evident, Japan; RRID:SCR_024783). It had a UPLXAPO 10x/0.4 lens (working distance 3.1 mm), a Hamamatsu ORCA-Flash 4.0 CMOS camera and VS200 ASW software (v3.4.1; Olympus). An X-Cite NOVEM 475 nm LED (Excelitas, PA, USA) lit up the Alexa Fluor 488 dye.

We looked through the overview pictures in QuPath (v0.4.2), a free, open-source program (Bankhead et al. 2017). We then chose the brain regions we wanted to study. For each region, we took a Z-stack of both the mGFP and the mRuby signals. A Z-stack is a series of pictures taken at different depths, from the top of the slice to the bottom.

Because of equipment shortages, we used two different confocal microscopes to take these pictures. A confocal microscope uses lasers to take sharp pictures at each depth. For mice 155, 156, 161 and 162, we used an inverted Zeiss LSM 880 confocal microscope (Carl Zeiss AG, Germany) with a Plan-Apochromat 40x/1.3 NA oil lens and ZEN Black software. We took the pictures with lasers of 458 and 561 nm, to see the Alexa Fluor 488 and 555 signals.

For all the other mice, we used a Leica Stellaris 5 confocal microscope (Leica Biosystems, Germany; RRID:SCR_024663) with a Plan-Apochromat 40x/1.3 NA oil lens and Leica Application Suite (LAS) X software. We took the pictures with lasers of 499 and 553 nm, to see the Alexa Fluor 488 and 555 signals. To measure how much mGFP and mRuby there was, we used a maximum intensity projection of each Z-stack. This is a single picture made from the brightest point at each position across all the depths.

For the experiments that followed fibres backward, we took stitched confocal pictures with the Leica Stellaris 5 confocal microscope. We used a Plan-Apochromat 20x/0.75 NA lens and LAS X software. We took the pictures with lasers of 405, 499, 552 and 649 nm. These showed the DAPI, Alexa Fluor 488, Opal 570 and Opal 690 signals, in that order.

### Lining up the brain pictures

For the experiments that followed fibres forward, we lined up the overview pictures of the slices with the Allen Mouse CCFv3 reference atlas (Wang et al. 2020b; RRID:SCR_020999). This atlas is a standard map of the mouse brain. We used QuickNII (v2.2; Puchades et al. 2019; RRID:SCR_016854) to allow for the angle at which we had cut the slices.

Slicing can stretch or squeeze the tissue a little. To correct for this, we made small, uneven adjustments to each lined-up slice with VisuAlign (v0.9; RRID:SCR_017978). We then laid the matching 40× high-magnification Z-stacks on top of the lined-up overview slices. In QuPath, we drew the regions where we could see mGFP or mRuby onto the 40× pictures. We later used these regions to measure the area of mGFP and mRuby. Examples of the lining-up are shown in Supplementary Fig. 7.

### Measuring and analysing the results

For the experiments that followed fibres forward, we measured the area of mGFP and mRuby with the ‘pixel classifier’ built into QuPath. This is a machine-learning tool that learns to tell apart areas that contain a signal from areas that do not. We gave it a random set of pictures from each experiment to learn from. We marked areas in these training pictures by hand as ‘positive’ or ‘negative’ for mGFP or mRuby. We kept going until the tool had learned the pattern well.

In some regions, the tool was not accurate enough. For these, we trained extra pixel classifiers and used them. To get the density, we divided the total area the tool found by the total area of the region. For each brain region, we included at least two measurements per mouse.

For the experiments that followed fibres backward, we drew the outlines of the lateral habenula and the zona incerta by hand. We found the cells with a DAPI-stained nucleus (DAPI + cells) in batches. To do this, we combined a custom computer script with QuPath’s built-in ‘positive cell detection’ tool. We found the cells carrying Rxfp3, Slc17a6 or Gad1 messages, and the cells carrying the eGFP signal, with QuPath’s built-in ‘object classifier’. This tool works in a similar way to the pixel classifier, but it sorts whole objects, such as cells. We gave it two pictures from each mouse to learn from. We marked cells by hand as ‘positive’ or ‘negative’ for the marker we were looking for, until the tool had learned the pattern well.

For Rxfp3, Slc17a6 and Gad1, we used a rough scoring method rather than an exact count. Each dot in the RNAscope picture stands for one genetic message (Wang et al. 2012). We counted a cell as positive for a marker if it had two or more glowing dots within 5 µm of its DAPI-stained nucleus (Ch’ng et al. 2019; Richards et al. 2025; Viden et al. 2022; Walker et al. 2021). We then used a custom script to apply the trained classifiers to every outlined region in every picture. The script sorted each DAPI + cell as ‘positive’ or ‘negative’ for each marker. Our QuPath scripts are available at https://github.com/BrandonKR1.

### Names of brain regions

The short names in Table 2 mostly follow the Mouse Brain Atlas in Stereotaxic Coordinates (Paxinos and Franklin 2001) or the Allen Mouse CCFv3 Reference Atlas (Wang et al. 2020b). There are some exceptions.

We split the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis into a lower part (BSTV) and a back part (BSTC). We did this because we saw no mGFP or mRuby signal in the upper and front parts of this structure. We split the lateral hypothalamic area into three zones from front to back: anterior, tuberal and mammillary. We named them as Hahn et al. (2019) did. We used the rostral periaqueductal gray (RPAG) to mark the part of the periaqueductal gray (PAG) that comes before the region starts to form columns.

## Results

### Where we injected the tracer

We wanted to know whether the LH/ZIRXFP3 cells in different parts of the lateral hypothalamus and zona incerta send their nerve fibres to different places across the brain. To find out, we injected a tracer virus into one side of the brain at a time. The virus only switches on in cells that carry the Cre gene, and it travels forward along the nerve fibres. Its full name is AAV-DJ-hSyn-FLEX-mGFP-synaptophysin-mRuby (Fig. 1A).

We injected it into four different areas of the lateral hypothalamus and zona incerta in mice that carry the Cre gene. The four areas were the front part of the lateral hypothalamus (ALH; 3 mice), the front part of the zona incerta (ZIR; 4 mice), the middle part of the zona incerta (ZII; 6 mice) and the back part of the zona incerta (ZIC; 4 mice). We used both male and female mice, but we did not compare the sexes, because the groups did not contain equal numbers of each sex (Supplementary Table 1).

When we injected the front part of the lateral hypothalamus, only a few green-glowing cells appeared there, and they stayed mostly within this area (Fig. 1B–D, top row, Supplementary Fig. 1).

When we injected the front part of the zona incerta, we found a thick, unbroken group of green-glowing cells. It stretched across the front part of the zona incerta and into the upper part of the lateral hypothalamus (Fig. 1B–D, second row, Supplementary Fig. 2). From here on, we call this group the ZIR/dmLH group. In these mice, green-glowing cells also sat between the front part of the zona incerta and the upper part of the lateral hypothalamus, just above and to the side of the fornix, a large bundle of nerve fibres (Supplementary Fig. 2). To keep things clear, we have given this zone a name: the incertohypothalamic area (IHy; Fig. 1D). It has no name in the standard mouse brain maps (Paxinos and Franklin 2001; Wang et al. 2020b).

When we injected the middle part of the zona incerta, the green-glowing cells were mostly in the front half of the upper and lower parts of the zona incerta. Now and then, though, we saw them near the border between the front part of the zona incerta and the middle part (Fig. 1D, third row, Supplementary Fig. 3). The front half of the upper part of the zona incerta held more of these cells than the front half of the lower part. It held 62.5% of all the green-glowing cells, give or take 5.3%, compared with 17.3% (give or take 2.1%) in the lower part. The back part of the front half of the upper and lower parts also held green-glowing cells, 38.8% (give or take 5.1%) of the total (Fig. 1B–D, bottom row; Supplementary Fig. 4).

The back part of the zona incerta gave a similar picture. Most of its green-glowing cells were in the upper part (72.1% of the total, give or take 6.4%) rather than the lower part (27.9%, give or take 6.4%).

### Broad patterns of where the nerve fibres go

Next, we asked whether the LH/ZIRXFP3 cells from each injection spot send their nerve fibres to different broad parts of the brain. For each group, we worked out two percentages. The first was the share of all green-glowing fibres that lay in each major brain region. The second was the share of all red-glowing endings that lay in that region.

The red glow is the more trustworthy sign of where a nerve fibre probably ends. A green-glowing fibre could simply pass through a region without stopping there. So, to keep things short, we describe only the red-glowing endings here, although both measures are shown in Fig. 2.

The two groups sent similar shares of their fibres to the diencephalon as a whole. This was 33.8% (give or take 10.0%) of the green-glowing fibres and 34.6% (give or take 9.9%) of the red-glowing endings. Within the diencephalon, though, the back part of the zona incerta leaned towards the thalamus rather than the hypothalamus. In every group, we saw no fibres in the hippocampus, amygdala or cerebral cortex. The cerebellar nuclei, deep inside the cerebellum, were lost while we prepared the tissue.

We also made maps of the whole brain for one typical mouse from each group. On these maps, the green-glowing fibres and red-glowing endings appear as simple yes-or-no outlines, laid over a standard reference map of the mouse brain (Fig. 4).

Usually, the red-glowing endings followed the same pattern as the green-glowing fibres but were less dense. Where the red glow did not, we point this out. #### The front part of the brain

##### Pallidum

The pallidum is a group of nuclei in the forebrain that help control movement. Most fibres going to the pallidum appeared in two of the four ZIR/dmLH mice (cases #164 and #165). The strongest fibres went to the nucleus of the diagonal band (Fig. 5). There, fibres running diagonally filled the whole length of the nucleus, from front to back, but were packed more tightly in its middle part (about 0.60 mm in front of Bregma).

These two mice also sent a moderate share of their fibres to the medial septal nucleus and the substantia innominata (Fig. 5). Every ZIR/dmLH mouse sent a small share to the lower part of the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis. In most mice injected in the front part of the lateral hypothalamus or in the middle and back parts of the zona incerta, the pallidum nuclei held little or no glow.

##### Striatum

The striatum is a group of nuclei in the forebrain that help control movement. In every group, it held little or no glow, with a few exceptions. One ZIR/dmLH mouse (case #165) sent a moderate share of its fibres to the lower third of the lateral septal nucleus (Fig. 5). #### The diencephalon

##### Preoptic hypothalamus

The preoptic hypothalamus lies just in front of the hypothalamus. Fibres went there most strongly in the ZIR/dmLH group. In these mice, a thick network of fibres covered most of the lateral preoptic area. It joined up with glow in the outer part of the medial preoptic area, the parastrial nucleus and the outer part of the substantia innominata (Fig. 6A). In the mice injected in the front part of the lateral hypothalamus or in the middle and back parts of the zona incerta, a small to moderate share of fibres ran along the whole length of the lateral preoptic area, especially on its lower inner side (Fig. 6B). The rest of the preoptic hypothalamus held only a few fibres.

##### Anterior hypothalamus

The anterior hypothalamus usually received a moderate share of fibres, and the pattern was much the same in every group. Fibres often ran diagonally, forming a continuous path across the inner part of the front part of the lateral hypothalamus and the outer part of the anterior hypothalamic area. Some fibres passed through the fornix (Fig. 7A).

Towards the front, there was no glow in the paraventricular hypothalamus. Further back (about 1.2 mm behind Bregma), a band of fibres crossed the upper edge of the anterior hypothalamic area without entering the paraventricular hypothalamus above it (Fig. 7A). The paraventricular hypothalamus held a small to moderate amount of green glow further back, except in the mice injected in the front part of the lateral hypothalamus. But it usually held little or no red glow. This suggests that these fibres were probably passing through, rather than ending there.

In most mice injected in the middle part of the zona incerta, a very thick network of fibres joined up with the front part of the zona incerta. It filled the undifferentiated zone between the front part of the zona incerta and the upper part of the lateral hypothalamus, which Sita and colleagues (2007) call the incertohypothalamic area (Fig. 7B). In the ZIR/dmLH group, the front part of the lateral hypothalamus held a very large amount of green glow. This was mainly because the green-glowing cell bodies themselves marked the injection spot.

##### Tuberal hypothalamus

The tuberal hypothalamus showed similar patterns in every group. A few fibres, mostly not overlapping, stretched across the middle part of the lateral hypothalamus. In the mice injected in the middle part of the zona incerta, however, a thick tangle of fibres also filled the upper part of the lateral hypothalamus, joining up with glow in the lower part of the zona incerta (Fig. 7C). Every group sent only a few fibres to the ventromedial hypothalamic nucleus. In the ZIR/dmLH group and the mice injected in the middle part of the zona incerta, a moderate share of fibres ran in the front part of the dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus, coming in from the middle from the zona incerta and the incertohypothalamic area (Fig. 7B).

##### Mammillary hypothalamus

The mammillary hypothalamus is the region around the mammillary bodies, small bumps at the back of the hypothalamus. Different injection spots sent fibres to its parts in different ways. The clearest difference was in the upper part of the premammillary nucleus. In the mice injected in the front part of the lateral hypothalamus and in the ZIR/dmLH group, a large share of fibres filled most of this region (Fig. 8A, B). In the back part of the zona incerta, only a small share went there (Fig. 8E). The middle part of the zona incerta also sent a small share to this region (Fig. 8C), except in case #179, which sent a large share, like the other two groups (Fig. 8D). In every case, the upper part of the premammillary nucleus on the opposite side of the brain held slightly less glow. Case #179 was the only mouse injected in the middle part of the zona incerta that had any green-glowing cell bodies in the lateral hypothalamus. So the fibres we saw in the premammillary nucleus probably came from RXFP3-carrying cells in the lateral hypothalamus.

##### Lateral habenula

The lateral habenula is a small brain region that helps process negative feelings. It was a key target for fibres from the same side of the brain and from the opposite side, especially in the ZIR/dmLH group and in the mice injected in the front part of the lateral hypothalamus. The ZIR/dmLH group sent the most green glow and red glow to the lateral habenula of all the groups, especially at its back end (Fig. 9A).

In the ZIR/dmLH group, the lateral habenula held a large share of all the green glow and red glow in the brain. In fact, it held about 15% of all the green glow in the brain, more than half of the green glow going to the thalamus. It also held about 21% of all the red glow in the brain, more than three-quarters of the red glow going to the thalamus (Fig. 9B). In the mice injected in the front part of the lateral hypothalamus, the lateral habenula held about 13% of all the green glow in the brain, about half of the green glow going to the thalamus. It held about 12% of all the red glow in the brain, more than half of the red glow going to the thalamus.

##### Upper thalamus

The upper thalamus was a key target for the mice injected in the middle and back parts of the zona incerta. The mice injected in the front part of the lateral hypothalamus and in the ZIR/dmLH group mostly avoided it.

Towards the front, the reuniens thalamic nucleus held a moderate share of green-glowing fibres in both the middle and back parts of the zona incerta (Fig. 11A). But the red-glowing endings told a different story. In the back part of the zona incerta, this nucleus held a moderate to large share of red-glowing endings, while in the middle part it held only a small to moderate share. This suggests that most of the reuniens thalamic nucleus's input comes from the back part of the zona incerta rather than the middle part.

In the back part of the zona incerta, a moderate to large share of fibres filled the middle parts of the upper thalamus, to the side of the lateral habenula. These were especially the centrolateral thalamic nucleus, the inner part of the laterodorsal thalamic nucleus and the lateral posterior thalamic nucleus (Fig. 11B). Further back, a thick band of fibres often crossed the upper part of the ventromedial thalamic nucleus, at the same level as the front tip of the superior cerebellar peduncle, a bundle of fibres linking the cerebellum to the brain (Fig. 11C). In both the middle and back parts of the zona incerta, a moderate to large share of fibres ran up and down in the lower part of the subparafascicular thalamic nucleus, joining up with glow in the neighbouring posterior hypothalamic area.

##### Lower thalamus

The lower thalamic nuclei were mainly targeted by the mice injected in the middle and back parts of the zona incerta. The back part of the zona incerta generally sent stronger fibres to parts of the geniculate complex, a group of nuclei that handle vision, than the middle part did. In the back part of the zona incerta, a large share of fibres joined up with glow in the outer part of the lower part of the zona incerta and reached the neighbouring ventral lateral geniculate nucleus. To a lesser extent, they also reached the intergeniculate leaf (Fig. 11D). Interestingly, there was a clear border between the intergeniculate leaf and the upper part of the lateral geniculate nucleus, which held no glow (Fig. 11D).

In both the middle and back parts of the zona incerta, a large share of fibres joined up with glow in the inner part of the lower part of the zona incerta and reached the neighbouring fields of Forel (Fig. 11E). However, red-glowing endings were only weakly present in three of the mice injected in the middle part of the zona incerta.

Mainly in the back part of the zona incerta, a thin band of fibres joined up with glow in the front part of the zona incerta and the front part of the upper and lower parts of the zona incerta. It ran up and down and ran along the border of the reticular thalamic nucleus and the neighbouring ventral posterolateral thalamic nucleus (Fig. 11F). To keep things simple, we counted glow with this pattern as belonging to the reticular thalamic nucleus. This accounts for most of the reticular thalamic nucleus glow in the back part of the zona incerta. Glow in the reticular thalamic nucleus itself was usually sparse, similar to the other groups.

#### The midbrain

##### Periaqueductal gray

The periaqueductal gray is a region in the midbrain that surrounds the cerebral aqueduct, a narrow channel. It was a key target for the mice injected in the middle and back parts of the zona incerta. Towards the front, fibres running up and down filled the front part of the periaqueductal gray (Fig. 13A, B) and the area above the oculomotor nucleus, which controls eye movements.

Further back, the two groups showed similar patterns. The ventrolateral column received the most fibres, followed by the lateral, dorsolateral and dorsomedial columns (Fig. 13C, D). However, the back part of the zona incerta always sent more fibres than the middle part to every column. The glow was generally stronger in the outer parts of each column, especially the lateral and ventrolateral columns, and weaker closer to the aqueduct (Fig. 13C, D).

##### Tegmentum

The tegmentum is the inner part of the midbrain. Many of its areas were key targets for the mice injected in the middle and back parts of the zona incerta. In most of the areas we looked at, the back part of the zona incerta sent stronger fibres than the middle part.

Towards the front, fibres joined up with the upper part of the front periaqueductal gray and filled the nucleus of the posterior commissure (Fig. 15A), the precommissural nucleus and the retroparafascicular nucleus. In the back part of the zona incerta, fibres mainly filled the inner part of the anterior pretectal nucleus. They also spread without any particular pattern into the inner, posterior and olivary pretectal nuclei (Fig. 15A). The middle part of the zona incerta sent only weak fibres to these areas.

Areas just below the front periaqueductal gray also received a moderate to large share of fibres. These included the nucleus of Darkschewitsch, the interstitial nucleus of Cajal and the Edinger-Westphal nucleus. In the middle of the tegmentum, fibres running diagonally filled only a few of the upper parts of the midbrain reticular nucleus, but gathered thickly around its centre. A thick band of fibres crossed the outer edge of the red nucleus and entered the inner part of the midbrain reticular nucleus (Fig. 15B). A separate band of a moderate share of fibres ran through the upper part of the midbrain reticular nucleus and ended in the sagulum nucleus.

In the lower parts of the tegmentum, a thick cluster of fibres sat in a small lower inner part of the compact part of the substantia nigra (Fig. 15B). This nucleus held no glow anywhere else. The ventral tegmental area also held a small share of glow throughout.

Further back, a large share of fibres joined up with the outer part of the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray and filled the inner part of the cuneiform nucleus from front to back (Fig. 15D). The ventral tegmental nucleus and the dorsal raphe nucleus both received a moderate share of fibres.

##### Superior colliculus

The superior colliculus is a region in the midbrain that helps with vision. The back part of the zona incerta sent the strongest fibres to its parts (Fig. 15C). In general, a moderate share of fibres filled the inner parts of the lower layers: the deep gray layer, the intermediate gray layer and the intermediate white layer. Now and then, we saw fibres in the outer parts of these layers. A small to moderate share of fibres filled the upper layers: the optic nerve layer and the superficial gray layer.

#### The hindbrain

##### Pons

The pons is a part of the hindbrain. In both the back part of the zona incerta and the middle part, the oral part of the pontine reticular nucleus received a huge share of fibres along its whole length (Fig. 16A). In the middle part of the zona incerta, the oral part of the pontine reticular nucleus held 71.5% (give or take 2.3%) of all the green glow in the pons and 28.3% (give or take 3.2%) of all the red glow in the pons. In the back part of the zona incerta, it held 56.5% (give or take 3.1%) of all the green glow in the pons and 21.5% (give or take 0.9%) of all the red glow in the pons (Fig. 16B).

In the front of the pons, thick bands of fibres crossed from the oral part of the pontine reticular nucleus to the median raphe nucleus, the reticulotegmental nucleus and the outer part of the pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (Fig. 16C). In the middle of the pons, the oral part of the pontine reticular nucleus joined up with glow in the back part of the pontine reticular nucleus and the nucleus raphe pontis. Further back, a large share of fibres filled the lower half of the nucleus incertus, joining up with a large share of fibres in the central gray of the pons (Fig. 16D). Interestingly, the fibres generally avoided the dorsal tegmental nucleus and the laterodorsal tegmental nucleus, which sit inside the central gray of the pons (Fig. 16D). The subcoeruleus nucleus and the sublaterodorsal nucleus held a moderate share of glow.

##### Medulla

The medulla is the lowest part of the brainstem. The middle and back parts of the zona incerta sent a small share of fibres to it, or a small to moderate share. However, a moderate to large share of fibres went to the magnocellular reticular nucleus, the abducens nucleus, which controls one of the eye muscles, and the raphe magnus nucleus. A moderate share also went to the front part of the gigantocellular reticular nucleus.

#### White matter

White matter is the brain's network of nerve fibres. In the mice with strong glow in the lateral habenula (mainly ZIR/dmLH case 172), we often saw fibres in the fasciculus retroflexus, a bundle of fibres linking the habenula to the midbrain, joining up with glow in the back part of the lateral habenula. In the ZIR/dmLH group, a moderate to large share of fibres ran steadily along the edges of the stria medullaris of the thalamus. In the back part of the zona incerta, a large share of fibres running up and down filled the trapezoid body, a bundle of hearing fibres, and pushed into the upper part of the pyramidal tract, a bundle of motor fibres, at the level of the gigantocellular reticular nucleus. In the middle and back parts of the zona incerta, a moderate to large share of fibres filled the medial lemniscus, a bundle of sensory fibres, at the level of the ventral tegmental area. This often joined up with glow in the lower part of the midbrain reticular nucleus (Fig. 13B).

## Discussion

In this study, we injected a tracer virus into four different spots in the lateral hypothalamus and zona incerta of mice that carry the Cre gene. The tracer travels forward along nerve fibres, and it only switches on in cells that carry the Cre gene. We then mapped where the nerve fibres went across the whole brain.

We sorted the injections into four groups, based on how far the virus spread. In the first group, which we call ALHRXFP3, the virus stayed within the front third of the lateral hypothalamus. In the second group, ZIR/dmLHRXFP3, it spread into the incertohypothalamic area, a zone where the zona incerta meets the hypothalamus, and into the upper, middle part of the lateral hypothalamus. In the third group, ZIIRXFP3, the virus stayed mostly within the front half of the dorsal and ventral parts of the zona incerta. In the fourth group, ZICRXFP3, it stayed mostly within the back half of those same two parts.

Looking at the big picture, we showed that cells from the ALHRXFP3 and ZIR/dmLHRXFP3 groups mainly send their fibres to regions of the diencephalon, the deep core of the brain that includes the hypothalamus and thalamus. Cells from the ZIIRXFP3 and ZICRXFP3 groups mostly send their fibres further down, to nuclei in the midbrain and pons. (A nucleus is a small, tightly packed group of nerve cells.)

Looking at single nuclei, we showed that each injection group produced its own pattern of connections. This was especially true for nuclei known to be involved in threats and defence. This fits with an earlier finding from our lab. When we switched on a large group of LH/ZIRXFP3 cells with a drug that acts on a genetically engineered receptor, the mice showed several different behaviours while remembering a fear they had learned. These included moving around more and jumping as if trying to escape (Richards et al. 2025). Taken together, our results suggest that LH/ZIRXFP3 cells send their fibres to different places across the brain depending on where they sit within these nuclei. This likely reflects the many different jobs these nerve cells do.

### Fibres going to the dorsal premammillary nucleus

The dorsal premammillary nucleus (PMD) was a key target in the ALHRXFP3 and ZIR/dmLHRXFP3 groups. It was also a key target in one ZIIRXFP3 case, where the virus had reached cells in the lateral hypothalamus. Several lines of evidence suggest that the fibres going to the PMD come from the lateral hypothalamus. On the other hand, we found that the main source of these fibres was the ZIR/dmLHRXFP3 cells.

This mismatch may come from the way we did the experiment. For example, in rodents, a connection from the lateral hypothalamus to the PMD is well documented (Comoli et al. 2000; Faturi et al. 2014; Goto et al. 2005; Hahn & Swanson 2012; Viellard et al. 2024). Yet only a few fibres to the PMD have been reported from dopamine cells in one part of the zona incerta, called A13, in one recent study (Bono et al. 2025). In rats, the fibres reported to go to the PMD come from two parts of the lateral hypothalamus: the part next to the dorsomedial hypothalamus, and the part above the fornix (Faturi et al. 2014; Hahn & Swanson 2012; Viellard et al. 2024). Standard mouse brain maps do not name these parts. However, they seem to overlap with the incertohypothalamic area we defined in our study. In the ZIR/dmLHRXFP3 cases, we saw many cell bodies there that glowed with the tracer and also stained for the tracer's protein. Still, to find out for certain where the LH/ZIRXFP3 fibres to the PMD come from, a backward-travelling tracer that only switches on in Cre-carrying cells should be injected into the PMD of these mice.

The PMD is a small nucleus in the hypothalamus. Most of its cells make the chemical messenger glutamate and also a hormone called cholecystokinin. These cells are switched on by many kinds of threats. These include breathing carbon dioxide (Johnson et al. 2011), meeting a predator (Melleu et al. 2022; Mendes-Gomes et al. 2020), and losing a fight with another animal (De Almeida et al. 2022; Faturi et al. 2014). Of special interest, switching on the PMD makes animals escape in ways that suit the situation (Laing et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2021).

We have shown that switching on LH/ZIRXFP3 cells with a drug that acts on a genetically engineered receptor makes some mice jump as if in panic. This happens in a fear chamber where the floor is a grid of bars, so the mouse cannot escape. It is possible that glutamate-making LH/RXFP3 cells switched on PMD cells further down the chain, allowing the mouse to escape in the right way, that is, by jumping to avoid the grid floor. Future studies should find out which chemical messengers the LH/RXFP3 cells that go to the PMD use. They should also switch this pathway on and off in different threatening situations, to work out its role in escape behaviour that suits the situation.

### Fibres going to the lateral habenula

The lateral habenula is a well-known target of the front part of the lateral hypothalamus (Hahn et al. 2022). In earlier work, we showed that LH/ZIRXFP3 cells send fibres to the lateral habenula. However, we did not find out exactly where in the lateral hypothalamus these fibres came from, or how they spread out inside the lateral habenula (Richards et al. 2025).

In this study, we found that ALHRXFP3 and ZIR/dmLHRXFP3 cells both send strong fibres to the lateral habenula, but to different parts of it. The lateral habenula is divided into smaller nuclei. The ALHRXFP3 cases mainly send fibres to the lateral nucleus (LHbL) and avoid two others, the lateral outer nucleus (LHbLO) and the medial posterior nucleus (LHbMPc). The ZIR/dmLHRXFP3 cases mainly send fibres to the medial nucleus (LHbM).

We also used a backward-travelling tracer and checked the chemical messengers the cells use. This showed that most of the fibres going to the lateral habenula came from a subset of cells across the lateral hypothalamus that carry both RXFP3 and the gene for the glutamate transporter (Slc17a6). They did not come from ZIR cells that carry RXFP3. Overall, our results show that the LH/RXFP3 cells that go to the lateral habenula are a subset of glutamate-making cells arranged in a map-like way. Those in the upper, middle part of the lateral hypothalamus mostly go to the medial nucleus, while those in the front part of the lateral hypothalamus mostly go to the lateral nucleus.

Our findings largely match a recent study. That study showed that the lateral hypothalamus contains several types of glutamate-making cells, each sitting in its own area and sending fibres to its own part of the lateral habenula (Calvigioni et al. 2023). What matters for our study is that it found two such types. One type carries a gene called Esr1. These cells sit in the upper, middle part of the lateral hypothalamus, send fibres to the medial nucleus, and avoid the medial posterior and lateral outer nuclei. This exactly matches the LH/ZIRXFP3 cells in the upper, middle part of the lateral hypothalamus. The other type makes a chemical messenger called neuropeptide-Y. These cells sit in the front part of the lateral hypothalamus and mostly end in the lateral nucleus, which matches the ALHRXFP3 cells. So it seems likely that the LH/ZIRXFP3 cells in the upper, middle part of the lateral hypothalamus are a subset of Esr1-carrying cells, and the ALHRXFP3 cells are a subset of neuropeptide-Y-making cells. However, future studies are needed to check this idea.

Several studies have shown that glutamate-making cells running from the lateral hypothalamus to the lateral habenula carry signals about things that animals dislike (Lazaridis et al. 2019; Lecca et al. 2017; Zheng et al. 2022). However, these cells are usually studied as if they were all the same. On the other hand, recent studies that recorded electrical activity in these cells found something different. When a foot was shocked, cells in the lateral nucleus became more active, while cells in the medial nucleus became less active (Congiu et al. 2019, 2023). So our discovery that LH/RXFP3 cells sitting in different places send fibres only to one of these two nuclei suggests that these two groups may play different parts in processing unpleasant experiences.

On top of this, the Esr1-carrying and neuropeptide-Y-making cells that go to the lateral habenula each play a different role in dislike. The Esr1-carrying cells drive place aversion, meaning an animal avoids a place it has just experienced as unpleasant, and this happens in real time. The neuropeptide-Y-making cells drive rearing, meaning standing up on the hind legs without support (Calvigioni et al. 2023). This suggests that it would not be surprising if separate groups of LH/RXFP3 cells worked in opposite ways.

### Fibres going to the periaqueductal gray

We showed that the lateral and ventrolateral parts of the periaqueductal gray (LPAG/VLPAG) received strong fibres from the ZIIRXFP3 and ZICRXFP3 cells, but not from the ALHRXFP3 and ZIR/dmLHRXFP3 cells. We also used a backward-travelling tracer and checked the chemical messengers the cells use. This showed that most of the fibres going to the ventrolateral part came from a subset of cells in the dorsal and ventral parts of the zona incerta that make the enzyme GAD1, which is used to make GABA. Taken together, we have shown that a subset of GABA-making ZIRXFP3 cells, sitting in a particular area, sends fibres to the lateral and ventrolateral parts of the periaqueductal gray.

Several studies show that GABA-making cells in the zona incerta send fibres widely across the periaqueductal gray (Ahmadlou et al. 2021; Liu et al. 2017; Tong et al. 2025; Venkataraman et al. 2019; Yu et al. 2021; Zhao et al. 2019). Again, these cells are often studied as if they were all the same. However, GABA-making cells in the zona incerta are made up of subsets that differ in their chemistry. Some make the enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase (Negishi et al. 2020; Venkataraman et al. 2021), some make a chemical messenger called tachykinin-1 (Ahmadlou et al. 2021), some make somatostatin (Li et al. 2021), some make parvalbumin (Wallén-Mackenzie et al. 2020), and many make other substances (Cheung et al. 2021; Li et al. 2021; Liu et al. 2017; Zhu et al. 2025). Some of these subsets send fibres to particular columns of the periaqueductal gray. For example, tachykinin-1-making cells go to the lateral and ventrolateral parts (Ahmadlou et al. 2021), calretinin-making cells go to the dorsal part (Li et al. 2021), and parvalbumin-making cells end along the side edge of the dorsal, lateral and ventrolateral parts (Wang et al. 2020a; Zhou et al. 2018).

Here we showed that RXFP3-carrying GABA-making cells in the zona incerta send fibres specifically to the lateral and ventrolateral parts, just like the tachykinin-1-making cells. Moreover, the GABA-making cells in the zona incerta send fibres to the periaqueductal gray in a map-like way. Cells in the middle of the zona incerta go to the lateral and ventrolateral parts, cells in the side go to the dorsal part, and cells in the ZIR go to the dorsal part (Yang et al. 2022). Scientists also widely accept that different columns of the periaqueductal gray do different jobs (Reis et al. 2023; Zhang et al. 2024). So it is clear that the GABA-making cells running from the zona incerta to the periaqueductal gray should not be treated as one single, uniform group. Future research should look at the different GABA-making groups, which differ in their chemistry and in where they sit, to work out their separate roles.

The strong fibres from the ZIIRXFP3 and ZICRXFP3 cells to the lateral and ventrolateral parts of the periaqueductal gray suggest that this pathway may control how defensive behaviours are carried out. It is widely accepted that switching on the lateral and ventrolateral parts makes animals freeze in defence (Fanselow et al. 1995; La-Vu et al. 2022). Switching on the dorsal part, on the other hand, makes animals jump as if in panic and try to escape (Deng et al. 2016; Evans et al. 2018).

Recent evidence suggests that freezing caused by the ventrolateral part comes from the activity of cells there that make glutamate (vGlut2). However, GABA-making cells in the ventrolateral part can calm the glutamate-making cells nearby and so stop freezing (Tovote et al. 2016). And switching on a small group of cells in the ventrolateral part that make both cholecystokinin and glutamate can drive escape behaviour (La-Vu et al. 2022). So GABA-making ZII/ZICRXFP3 cells may control either freezing or active escape in response to threats, depending on which particular ventrolateral cells they target. These targets, which are defined by the cells' chemistry, still need to be found.

This pathway may also control how fear is learned, not just how fear is shown. When the ventrolateral part was switched off with a drug that acts on a genetically engineered receptor, mice had trouble learning to stop a reward they had learned to expect (Arico et al. 2017). This behaviour does not depend on the periaqueductal gray to happen (Amorapanth et al. 1999). So this suggests that the problem was a failure to learn the link between the reward and the signal, rather than a failure to show fear.

### Other important connections

Looking at the big picture, the ALHRXFP3 and ZIR/dmLHRXFP3 cases mostly sent fibres to areas of the diencephalon, and each group had its own pattern of connections further back in the brain. In particular, the ZIR/dmLHRXFP3 cases alone sent fibres to areas of the basal forebrain (the lateral, medial and diagonal septal nuclei, and the substantia innominata) and to the preoptic part of the hypothalamus (the lateral and medial preoptic areas). Interestingly, studies that have shown a role for the lateral hypothalamus in the basal forebrain or preoptic nuclei looked at cells that make melanin-concentrating hormone or orexin (De Luca et al. 2022; Jego et al. 2013; Ma et al. 2023). These cells do not carry RXFP3 (Richards et al. 2025). One study has shown that GABA-making fibres from the lateral hypothalamus to the diagonal band drive feeding and reduce anxiety (Cassidy et al. 2019), but no other studies have tested what these pathways do. Many studies, including ours, have traced the nerve fibres to show that these connections exist. So future studies should try to work out what these connections do.

In contrast, the ZIIRXFP3 and ZICRXFP3 cases mostly sent fibres further down, to several regions of the midbrain and hindbrain that are strongly involved in arousal, meaning being awake and alert. These include the pedunculopontine tegmentum (PPTg), the nucleus incertus (NI) and the central gray of the pons (CGPn) (Dugan et al. 2023; Kroeger et al. 2022; Ma et al. 2017; Ryan et al. 2011; Wei et al. 2024). One result stood out. The fibres to the oral part of the pontine reticular nucleus (PnO) were especially dense, making up about a quarter of all the fibres from the ZIIRXFP3 and ZICRXFP3 cases.

A GABA-making pathway from the zona incerta to the PnO is well known, but only a handful of studies have looked at what it does in different situations (Ahmadlou et al. 2021; Zhao et al. 2019; Zhu et al. 2025). In one study, scientists used light to switch on the endings of GABA-making cells in the zona incerta that carry a gene called Pde11a, inside the PnO. This made animals more awake. It suggests that a subset of GABA-making cells in the zona incerta raises arousal by calming the PnO (Zhu et al. 2025). So it is possible that GABA-making ZII/ZICRXFP3 cells may control PnO activity to raise arousal when the surroundings demand it.

The ZIIRXFP3 and ZICRXFP3 cases also sent strong fibres to regions known to produce panic-like defensive behaviours. These include the superior colliculus (SC), the cuneiform nucleus (CnF) and the posterior hypothalamus (PH) (Biagioni et al. 2012; Bindi et al. 2023; Caggiano et al. 2018; Da Silva Soares et al. 2019; Falconi-Sobrinho et al. 2017). So the fibres from ZII/ZICRXFP3 cells to arousal-promoting regions may be needed for an animal to make active defensive responses to immediate threats.

It is well known that LH and ZI cells send their fibres to different places depending on where they sit (Hahn and Swanson 2010; Yang et al. 2022). RXFP3 is found widely across both nuclei, so it is not surprising that our injection groups also followed this rule. Even so, by tracing only the RXFP3-carrying cells within these areas, we found several clear differences from earlier studies of brain connections. In particular, the zona incerta is known to send strong fibres to the central nucleus of the amygdala (Reardon and Mitrofanis 2000; Wagner et al. 1995) and to many sensory areas of the cortex (Lin et al. 1990). These fibres were clearly missing in our study. Likewise, the front part of the lateral hypothalamus has been shown to send strong fibres to several nuclei in the hindbrain (Hahn and Swanson 2010). These were also not seen in the ALHRXFP3 or ZIR/dmLHRXFP3 groups.

### Points about our methods

We have shown before that the RXFP3-Cre mice used in this study are very precise, but that the Cre gene is not switched on in many of the cells that carry RXFP3. Only about 20% of the cells in the lateral hypothalamus and zona incerta that make the RXFP3 gene's message also make the Cre gene's message (Richards et al. 2025). So the Cre-dependent tracer virus we used is unlikely to have captured all the RXFP3-carrying cells in this region.

To find the likely endings of nerve fibres, we used a virus that makes a red glowing protein called mRuby when the cell makes a protein called synaptophysin. Synaptophysin is found in large amounts in the small endings of nerve fibres, but it is also found along the main fibre and in the tiny bubbles that carry material along it (Nakata et al., 1998). So a small dot of mRuby does not necessarily mean there is a nerve fibre ending, although this is more likely where many dots are packed together.

Finally, brain slices can be cut at a slant and can be stretched or squashed, which can make them look different from the standard brain map. To deal with this, we lined up our brain slices, cut across the brain from front to back, with the CCFv3 brain map, so we could mark out brain regions. We did not use stains that show the structure of the tissue, such as DAPI or Nissl, to help with this. In our experience, the computer tools QuickNii and VisuAlign give a more reliable way to find the edges of regions in flat pictures of brain slices. This is because they let us adjust the brain map to match the common distortions that happen while tissue is prepared, such as the angle of the cut, tearing and stretching. Supplementary Fig. 7 shows this process, and Fig. 4 shows where the fibres landed on the adjusted brain map.

## Conclusion

This study is the first to show that nerve fibres vary in where they go within a fairly continuous group of RXFP3-carrying cells in the zona incerta and lateral hypothalamus. Future studies should keep this in mind when they look at the connections of RXFP3-carrying cells in other parts of the brain where RXFP3 is common, such as the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BST) and the lateral septal nucleus (LS). They should not assume that all these cells send their fibres to the same places. This variety in where the fibres go is likely to lead to variety in what the cells do, and this deserves further study.
